bairuixiang.name: Bai Rui Xiang (White Daphne Fragrance)
bairuixiang.aroma: Sweet, woody-spicy, with nutty, fruity, and floral notes.
bairuixiang.taste: Dense, gently sweet, silky, with a hint of fruit acidity and spice; long finish.
bairuixiang.effect: Warming, clarifies the mind, relaxes the body while staying alert.
bairuixiang.story: Named after the winter daphne flower of southern China. Grown in the Wuyi reserve, birthplace of cliff oolongs. Excellent for ceremony, meditation, study, or focused work — relaxed body, engaged mind.
bairuixiang.brewing: Gongfu style in porous clay for heavily oxidized oolongs. ~6 g per 120 ml, 95°C, short infusions. 7–8 steeps.

dahongpao.name: Da Hong Pao (Big Red Robe)
dahongpao.aroma: Berry and nut, hints of chocolate, flowers, and wood.
dahongpao.taste: Silky, juicy, full-bodied, berry brightness, refreshing long aftertaste.
dahongpao.effect: Inner clarity and calm; relaxes the body, clears the head.
dahongpao.story: A landmark Chinese tea with over a thousand years of history. From the Wuyi national reserve, organic cultivation. Three generations of oolong specialists — exceptional quality, rarely matched in Ukraine.
dahongpao.brewing: Gongfu in porous clay. 6–8 g per 120 ml, 95–100°C. Start ~10 sec, lengthen each steep to ~2 min. About 9–10 infusions.

dancong.name: Fen Huang Dan Cong (Phoenix Mountain single bush)
dancong.taste: Rich, sweet, structured, fresh berry acidity.
dancong.effect: Tonifying, warming, stimulates focus and energy.
dancong.story: From Chaozhou, home of gongfu cha. One of China's four famous oolongs. Vivid, memorable character — ideal for daily drinking or beginners who want a bold introduction. Great for study and work.
dancong.brewing: 95–100°C in porcelain gaiwan or clay. 5 g per 100 ml, first steep 7–10 sec, increase time. 7–8 steeps.

dianhong.name: Dian Hong
dianhong.story: One of the most expressive red teas, popular in the West since the late 20th century. Distinct flavor and golden buds — a perfect introduction to red tea.
dianhong.brewing: 4–5 g per 100 ml at 90–100°C in gaiwan or clay. Western style: 1 g per 200 ml boiling water.

fudingbaicha.name: Fu Ding Bai Cha
fudingbaicha.aroma: Gentle sweet florals woven with fruit.
fudingbaicha.taste: Delicate, evolving sweetness; many infusions reveal depth.
fudingbaicha.effect: Calming, clarifying; low caffeine — suitable evening cup in warm seasons.
fudingbaicha.story: Classic white tea from the birthplace of white tea in eastern Fujian. Carefully picked buds and leaves. Brew slightly below boiling; porcelain, clay, or glass all work well.
fudingbaicha.brewing: Let water cool below boiling so it does not scald the leaf. Porcelain or glass; many re-steeps.

gongtingshupuer.name: Gong Ting Shu Pu-er (Palace ripe pu-er)
gongtingshupuer.taste: Smooth, sweet, light woodiness, dried fruit hint.
gongtingshupuer.effect: Warms, softens the mind, gently energizes the body.
gongtingshupuer.story: Fermented pu-er from palace-grade buds — dense, smooth, and rich. Shu pu-er is gentle on an empty stomach and supports digestion. Best morning or first half of the day.
gongtingshupuer.brewing: 95°C, clay or gaiwan. 6 g per 100 ml, ~10 sec first steep, lengthen. 6–8 infusions.

jinjunmei.name: Jin Jun Mei (Golden Eyebrows)
jinjunmei.aroma: Fresh bread, cane sugar, vanilla, orchid.
jinjunmei.effect: Warming, uplifting; lightly relaxing in smaller cups.
jinjunmei.story: Refined Wuyi red tea named for its golden, downy leaves. Wonderful entry point to Chinese tea — each steep shifts the flavor palette.
jinjunmei.brewing: 4 g per 100 ml at 90–95°C in gaiwan or clay. Western: half teaspoon per 200 ml, 15–20 sec.

laoshupuer.name: Lao Shu Shu Pu-er (old-tree ripe, 2003)
laoshupuer.aroma: Mature, nutty-balsamic, dried fruit, dark chocolate.
laoshupuer.taste: Velvety, balanced sweet and dried fruit, spicy long finish.
laoshupuer.effect: Warms, relaxes awareness while pu-er energizes body and mind.
laoshupuer.story: Twenty-one years of aging — for collectors and serious shu lovers. Balanced and warming; ideal winter–spring. A benchmark for quality ripe pu-er.
laoshupuer.brewing: 95–100°C, clay or gaiwan. 7 g per 100 ml, ~10 sec first steep. Up to 10 infusions.

longjin.name: Long Jing (Dragon Well)
longjin.taste: Soft, buttery, sweet, juicy, long finish.
longjin.story: Among China's most famous greens — flat "sparrow tongue" leaves. Over 1,500 years of craft; noted in Lu Yu's tea classic. High in vitamin C and antioxidants.
longjin.brewing: 75–85°C, porcelain or glass. 4 g per 100 ml, short infusions, up to 6 steeps.

rougui.name: Rou Gui (Cinnamon)
rougui.aroma: Deep, bready-spicy, cinnamon, bark, berry, chocolate.
rougui.taste: Sweet, juicy, light bite, dried cherry, cinnamon, vanilla.
rougui.effect: Warmth, calm steadiness — like after meditation.
rougui.story: A beloved Wuyi cultivar since the Qing dynasty, roasted with "high fire." Ceremonial tea with a bright, layered profile.
rougui.brewing: 95°C, porcelain or porous clay. 6 g per 100 ml, lengthening infusions. 6–8 steeps.

tieguanyin.name: Tie Guan Yin (Iron Goddess of Mercy)
tieguanyin.taste: Full, refreshing, silky, light fruit acidity, long finish.
tieguanyin.effect: Eases fatigue and tension; nourishes clarity.
tieguanyin.story: China's best-known oolong, legends dating to the 7th–9th centuries. Distinct aroma even for beginners. Rich in vitamins and minerals; harmonizing, peaceful state.
tieguanyin.brewing: 85–90°C, porcelain gaiwan or clay. 6 g per 100 ml, lengthening steeps. Up to 10 infusions.

xiaozhong.name: Xiao Zhong (Lapsang Souchong)
xiaozhong.taste: Soft, velvety, light acidity, rose hip and dried fruit.
xiaozhong.effect: Gentle stimulation, warming; milder cups relax.
xiaozhong.story: Classic Fujian red tea, known in the West and even served in the British Parliament. Everyday cup with depth — morning or evening with friends.

yundeshengpuer.name: Yunnan Sheng Pu-er
yundeshengpuer.taste: Fine, juicy, oily-sweet, light wood astringency, long finish.
yundeshengpuer.effect: Clears the mind, charges the body.
yundeshengpuer.story: Fresh sheng from old tea trees — soft taste, strong pu-er effect. For ceremony, focus, or gatherings. Prized in China; ages beautifully when stored well. Spring–summer tea that cools and energizes.
yundeshengpuer.brewing: 90–95°C, clay or gaiwan. 5 g per 100 ml, ~5 sec first steep. About 10 infusions.
